readings.title: How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin
readings.challenge: Follow a rude act and its delayed revenge, and enjoy a long phrase that keeps coming back.
readings.focus: A small, patient cook gets even with a huge, rude animal.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. A Superior Comestible is a very fine thing to eat; a sloka is a verse in an old Indian form; a waterproof is a raincoat; the P. and O. was a line of passenger steamships. The places at the end are real and made-up names mixed together.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Parsee is a member of the Parsi community of India, whose ancestors came from Persia; Kipling draws him as a comic figure, and “more-than-oriental splendour” uses an old word for the lands of Asia. These belong to Kipling’s time.

excerpt.locator: “How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin,” the whole story with its closing verse; opens “ONCE upon a time, on an uninhabited island on the shores of the Red Sea, there lived a…”; closes “…Suez For the likes of you and me Ever to go In a P. and O. And call on the Cake-Parsee!”.

questions.prompt: What did the Rhinoceros do to the Parsee’s cake? What does the narrator say about his manners?
facilitatorNotes: He knocked over the stove, spiked the cake on his horn and ate it. He “had no manners then, and he has no manners now, and he never will have any manners”: the narrator says it as if it were a law of nature.
evidence: he spiked that cake on the horn of his nose, and he ate it,
he had no manners then, and he has no manners now, and he never will have any manners.

questions.prompt: How was the Rhinoceros’s skin different in those days?
facilitatorNotes: It fitted tight with no wrinkles, buttoned underneath with three buttons, and could be taken off like a raincoat.
evidence: In those days it buttoned underneath with three buttons and looked like a waterproof.

questions.prompt: How did the Parsee get even? Why didn’t he simply fight the Rhinoceros?
facilitatorNotes: He filled the skin with stale, tickly cake-crumbs and burned currants while the Rhinoceros bathed, then waited up his palm tree. He is far smaller than the Rhinoceros; he wins by patience and a trick.
evidence: he rubbed that skin just as full of old, dry, stale, tickly cake-crumbs and some burned currants as ever it could possibly hold.

questions.prompt: After the Parsee’s rhyme, the narrator says “there was a great deal more in that than you would think.” What was the “more”?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme was a warning that came true: taking the cake led to the crumbs, the folds and the bad temper that, the story says, every rhinoceros has to this day. Readers may also say the rhyme sounds like a curse.
evidence: And there was a great deal more in that than you would think.
from that day to this every rhinoceros has great folds in his skin and a very bad temper,

questions.prompt: Kipling repeats “from whose hat the rays of the sun were reflected in more-than-oriental splendour.” Why might a storyteller keep repeating a long phrase?
facilitatorNotes: It is fun to say aloud, it makes the Parsee easy to picture, and listeners start to wait for it. In a story meant to be told “just so,” the repeats are part of the music. Some listeners find it funnier each time.
evidence: from whose hat the rays of the sun were reflected in more-than-oriental splendour.

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — ’satiable curtiosity (part 1)
readings.challenge: Enjoy the repeated phrases, and notice what happens every single time the Elephant’s Child asks a question.
readings.focus: A young elephant’s curiosity is punished again and again, yet sends him on a long journey.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. Long ago, this story says, elephants had no trunks. “’Satiable curtiosity” is the narrator’s way of saying insatiable curiosity, a curiosity that is never satisfied. “Dretful” means dreadful; “promiscuous parts” here means “all sorts of places around here.” Graham’s Town, Kimberley and Khama’s Country are places in southern Africa.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The young elephant is spanked by every relative he questions; spanking was a common punishment in Kipling’s time.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from the beginning through his meeting with the Python, ending “what he thought was a log of wood”; opens “IN the High and Far-Off Times the Elephant, O Best Beloved, had no trunk. He had only a…”; closes “…very edge of the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Elephant’s Child do with his “’satiable curtiosity,” and what happens each time?
facilitatorNotes: He asks question after question about everything, and every relative spanks him for it. “And still he was full of ’satiable curtiosity!” repeats like a chorus.
evidence: he asked ever so many questions.
and all his uncles and his aunts spanked him.

questions.prompt: Which question brings the biggest spanking of all? Why might everyone say “Hush!”?
facilitatorNotes: “What does the Crocodile have for dinner?” They may be afraid of the Crocodile, or of the answer, since a crocodile might eat a young elephant. The story lets readers guess.
evidence: What does the Crocodile have for dinner?
Then everybody said, 'Hush!' in a loud and dretful tone,

questions.prompt: Find the long phrase Kipling repeats about the river. Why do you think he repeats it?
facilitatorNotes: “The great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees.” It sounds like a chant, is fun to say together, and makes the place feel far away and important.
evidence: the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees,

questions.prompt: The part ends when he treads on “what he thought was a log of wood.” What do you predict, and which clue earlier in the story points to it?
facilitatorNotes: It is probably the Crocodile: the narrator has told us he “had never seen a Crocodile, and did not know what one was like,” so he would not recognize one.
evidence: this 'satiable Elephant's Child had never seen a Crocodile, and did not know what one was like.
till he trod on what he thought was a log of wood

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — the tug-of-war (part 2)
readings.challenge: Read the funny voices aloud, and work out what the long, grand names really mean.
readings.focus: Curiosity nearly costs the Elephant’s Child everything, and leaves him with something new.
readings.context: Recap: the Elephant’s Child, who is spanked for every question he asks, has travelled to the Limpopo River to find out what the Crocodile has for dinner. A python has spanked him too. Now he has stepped on what he thought was a log. Crocodile tears are pretend tears; an ulster is a long overcoat; a man-of-war is a warship; to vitiate is to spoil; “hijjus” means hideous, terribly.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Crocodile tries to eat the Elephant’s Child and stretches his nose painfully.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from “But it was really the Crocodile” through the three days’ wait, ending “same as all Elephants have to-day”; opens “But it was really the Crocodile, O Best Beloved, and the Crocodile winked one eye—like…”; closes “…Crocodile had pulled it out into a really truly trunk same as all Elephants have to-day.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Crocodile prove who he is? What is odd about that proof?
facilitatorNotes: He weeps crocodile tears “to show it was quite true.” Crocodile tears are fake tears, so his proof is really a warning sign. Listeners may spot the danger before the Elephant’s Child does.
evidence: he wept crocodile-tears to show it was quite true.

questions.prompt: Why does the Elephant’s Child say, “Led go! You are hurtig be!” Read it aloud the way he would.
facilitatorNotes: The Crocodile is holding his nose, so his words come out blocked: “Let go! You are hurting me!” Holding one’s own nose and saying it shows how Kipling spelled the sound.
evidence: 'Led go! You are hurtig be!'

questions.prompt: The Python calls the Crocodile two grand names. What are they, and why do they fit?
facilitatorNotes: “Your acquaintance in the large-pattern leather ulster”: his scaly hide looks like a big leather coat. “Self-propelling man-of-war with the armour-plated upper deck”: he is huge, armored and moves through water like a warship. The Python never says anything simply.
evidence: your acquaintance in the large-pattern leather ulster
yonder self-propelling man-of-war with the armour-plated upper deck

questions.prompt: The Elephant’s Child waits for his nose to shrink, and the Python says, “Some people do not know what is good for them.” What does the Python know that the Elephant’s Child does not yet know?
facilitatorNotes: That the stretched nose is not a disaster: it is a useful trunk, “same as all Elephants have to-day.” Some readers may feel sorry for him first; both feelings fit.
evidence: Some people do not know what is good for them.
the Crocodile had pulled it out into a really truly trunk same as all Elephants have to-day.

readings.title: The Elephant’s Child — ’vantages, and the way home (part 3)
readings.challenge: List what a new trunk can do, then judge what the Elephant’s Child does with it.
readings.focus: A painful accident turns out to be useful, and the Elephant’s Child goes home to settle the score.
readings.context: Recap: the Crocodile caught the curious Elephant’s Child by his small nose and pulled until, with the Python’s help, he got free; but his nose has stretched into a long trunk. He has waited three days for it to shrink. To hove is to throw; a pachyderm is a thick-skinned animal such as an elephant; a fly-whisk is a brush for flicking away flies.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. The Elephant’s Child gets revenge by spanking and roughly treating his whole family.

excerpt.locator: “The Elephant's Child,” from the fly on the third day to the end of the story, with the verse “I keep six honest serving-men”; opens “At the end of the third day a fly came and stung him on the shoulder, and before he knew…”; closes “…second she opens her eyes— One million Hows, two million Wheres, And seven million Whys!”.

questions.prompt: What three “’vantages” does the Python point out? Why couldn’t the Elephant’s Child do these with his old nose?
facilitatorNotes: Swatting a fly, plucking grass to eat, and slapping a cool mud-cap on his head. His old “mere-smear nose” could not reach or grip anything.
evidence: 'Vantage number one!' said the Bi-Coloured-Python-Rock-Snake.
he schlooped up a schloop of mud from the banks of the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo,

questions.prompt: What does he do on the way home that makes him a “Tidy Pachyderm”?
facilitatorNotes: He picks up all the melon rinds he dropped on the way to the river, when he had no way to pick them up.
evidence: he picked up the melon rinds that he had dropped on his way to the Limpopo—for he was a Tidy Pachyderm.

questions.prompt: When his family wants to spank him again, what does he do? Is it fair, or has he become just as bad as they were?
facilitatorNotes: He spanks them all, throws the Baboon into a hornets’ nest and pulls the Ostrich’s feathers, but never lets anyone touch the Kolokolo Bird, who helped him. The narrator calls him “that bad Elephant’s Child,” yet in the end “nobody spanked anybody any more.” Readers may argue it is fair payback, or that he has turned into a bully.
evidence: Then that bad Elephant's Child spanked all his dear families for a long time,
but he never let any one touch Kolokolo Bird.

questions.prompt: The verse at the end names “six honest serving-men.” Who are they really, and who is the “person small” who keeps ten million?
facilitatorNotes: They are the question words: What, Where, When, How, Why and Who. (This printing repeats “Where” in the fourth line, where most printings have “Why.”) The person small is a curious child who never stops asking, much like the Elephant’s Child; Kipling may mean his own daughter.
evidence: I keep six honest serving-men;
One million Hows, two million Wheres,

readings.title: The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo
readings.challenge: Listen for a wish that grows, a chase that repeats, and a short line that answers every change.
readings.focus: A proud animal gets exactly what he asked for, in a way he did not expect.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. The adult reads this one aloud; the child can join in on “He had to!” Inordinate means far too much; spinifex, mulga, blue gums and ti-trees are Australian plants; a salt-pan is a dried-up salty lake; a dingo is an Australian wild dog. “Played Old Scratch with” means ruined.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation. Nqa, Nquing and Nqong are gods Kipling invented for the story; they are not the beliefs of Aboriginal Australians.

excerpt.locator: “The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo,” the whole story with its closing verse; opens “NOT always was the Kangaroo as now we do behold him, but a Different Animal with four…”; closes “…But your legs would develop terrific— Yes, my importunate son, You'd be a Marvellous Kid!”.

questions.prompt: What did Kangaroo ask each of the three gods? How does his wish grow each time?
facilitatorNotes: Nqa: make me different from all other animals by five o’clock. Nquing: different, and wonderfully popular. Nqong: different, popular and “wonderfully run after.” Each time he asks for more.
evidence: Make me different from all other animals by five this afternoon.
make me popular and wonderfully run after by five this afternoon.

questions.prompt: How does Nqong grant the wish? Why is it a trick?
facilitatorNotes: He sends Dingo to chase Kangaroo: “run after” comes true word for word. Kangaroo meant admired; Nqong takes it literally.
evidence: He wants to be popular and very truly run after. Dingo, make him so!

questions.prompt: What short line keeps answering the story, and what does it mean each time?
facilitatorNotes: “He had to!” Kangaroo has no choice: the chase forces every change, from aching legs to hopping on two. Read it together each time it comes.
evidence: He had to!

questions.prompt: At the end, Kangaroo and Dingo each say, “That’s your fault.” Whose fault is it, in your view?
facilitatorNotes: Kangaroo asked for it, as Nqong reminds him; Nqong chose a hard way to grant it; Dingo only did as he was told and still has no dinner. Readers can blame different characters if they give a reason from the story.
evidence: didn't you ask me to make you different from all other animals, as well as to make you very truly sought after?
each said, 'That's your fault.'

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — which is which? (part 1)
readings.challenge: Untangle sentences that are tangled on purpose, and keep track of who is who.
readings.focus: Two small animals defend themselves by confusing a hungry jaguar with words.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. Turbid means muddy; the Amazon is the great river of South America; a jaguar is a big spotted cat. “To save my spots” is the Jaguar’s way of saying “for the life of me.”
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from the beginning through the Jaguar’s paw full of prickles; opens “THIS, O Best Beloved, is another story of the High and Far-Off Times. In the very middle…”; closes “…scratched his head with his un-prickly paw—'how do I know that this other is Tortoise?'”.

questions.prompt: What did Mother Jaguar tell her son about catching hedgehogs and tortoises?
facilitatorNotes: Drop a hedgehog into the water so it uncoils; scoop a tortoise out of its shell with your paw. Her advice only works if he can tell them apart.
evidence: when you find a Hedgehog you must drop him into the water and then he will uncoil,
when you catch a Tortoise you must scoop him out of his shell with your paw.

questions.prompt: Why can’t Painted Jaguar tell which animal is which?
facilitatorNotes: Both have hidden themselves: one curled into a ball, the other drew into its shell. He admits, “I can’t tell.”
evidence: Now which of you is Hedgehog and which is Tortoise? because to save my spots, I can't tell.

questions.prompt: How do Stickly-Prickly and Slow-Solid confuse the Jaguar? Try reading one of their versions of his mother’s advice aloud.
facilitatorNotes: They scramble the words of her advice into nonsense, so he begins to doubt what he remembers. Reading it aloud shows how tangled it is.
evidence: Perhaps she said that when you uncoil a Tortoise you must shell him out of the water with a scoop,

questions.prompt: Stickly-Prickly says, “you can scoop me out of my shell if you like.” Why is that a clever trick, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: It makes the Jaguar think he must be the Tortoise, so he grabs with his paw and gets a pawful of prickles; Stickly-Prickly is knocked away into the dark. The Jaguar learns which one he is not, but still cannot be sure about the other.
evidence: 'Aha!' said Painted Jaguar. 'Now I know you're Tortoise.
Jaguar's paddy-paw was just filled with prickles.

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — the truthful Tortoise (part 2)
readings.challenge: Follow a character who tells the truth in a way that makes it hard to believe.
readings.focus: The Tortoise escapes by telling the truth, but Mother Jaguar gives her son a rule he cannot forget.
readings.context: Recap: Painted Jaguar wants to eat Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog and Slow-Solid Tortoise, but cannot tell which is which. They tangled up his mother’s advice, and when he grabbed the one he thought was Tortoise, he got a paw full of prickles. Now he turns to Slow-Solid. To be “mixy” is the Jaguar’s word for muddled.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from “But I am Tortoise” through the Jaguar’s rhyme; opens “'But I am Tortoise,' said Slow-and-Solid. 'Your mother was quite right. She said that you…”; closes “…can swim— Slow-Solid, that's him! Curls up, but can't swim— Stickly-Prickly, that's him!'”.

questions.prompt: Slow-and-Solid tells the Jaguar how to make him swim away. Why doesn’t the Jaguar believe him?
facilitatorNotes: He is so muddled that he decides the opposite of whatever the Tortoise wants must be right: “as you seem so anxious to be dropped I think you don’t want to be dropped.” So he does exactly what lets the Tortoise escape.
evidence: if you want to see me swim away you've only got to drop me into the water.
as you seem so anxious to be dropped I think you don't want to be dropped.

questions.prompt: Read aloud the speech beginning “Well, suppose you say that I said that she said.” What is the Tortoise trying to do?
facilitatorNotes: Tie the Jaguar’s thinking in knots so that he gives up trusting his own memory. It works: the Jaguar says he does not know whether he is on his head or his tail.
evidence: if she said what you said I said she said, it's just the same as if I said what she said she said.

questions.prompt: Mother Jaguar gives new, clear rules. What are they, and why do they worry the two friends?
facilitatorNotes: A hedgehog curls into a ball with prickles; a tortoise cannot curl, only draw in. The rules are simple enough that “even Painted Jaguar can’t forget” them, so the friends’ tricks will not work again.
evidence: A Tortoise can't curl himself up,
Even Painted Jaguar can't forget those directions.

questions.prompt: Painted Jaguar turns his mother’s rules into a rhyme. Why might a rhyme help him? How could the two friends defeat it?
facilitatorNotes: Rhymes are easy to remember. The friends could only beat it by changing what they can do; readers may predict that each will learn the other’s trick.
evidence: Can't curl, but can swim— Slow-Solid, that's him!

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — practice in the river (part 3)
readings.challenge: Notice a word that keeps repeating, and spot the changes before the characters do.
readings.focus: Two friends teach each other their own skills, and their bodies begin to change.
readings.context: Recap: Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog and Slow-Solid Tortoise escaped Painted Jaguar by confusing him, but his mother taught him a rhyme: a tortoise can’t curl but can swim; a hedgehog curls up but can’t swim. Now the friends make a plan. A chestnut-burr is the prickly case of a chestnut; a side-stroke is a way of swimming.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from “He'll never forget that” through the friends’ plan to find the Jaguar; opens “'He'll never forget that this month of Sundays,' said Stickly-Prickly. 'Hold up my chin,…”; closes “…of being able to swim. Oh, won't Painted Jaguar be surprised! Let's go and find him.'”.

questions.prompt: What does each friend decide to learn, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Stickly-Prickly will learn to swim and Slow-Solid will learn to curl up, so the Jaguar’s rhyme will no longer tell them apart. “It may be useful,” they both say.
evidence: I'm going to try to learn to swim. It may be useful.
I'll see what I can do towards curling up. It may be useful.

questions.prompt: Find the word the friends keep saying to each other. What does it show about how they help each other?
facilitatorNotes: “Excellent!” Each praises the other’s small progress, holds up a chin or unlaces a plate. They are patient teachers.
evidence: 'Excellent!' said Slow-and-Solid;
You'll make a fine swimmer yet,

questions.prompt: How are their bodies changing as they practise? Find the clue about pine-cones.
facilitatorNotes: The Tortoise’s plates now overlap, and the Hedgehog’s prickles are melting together so he looks like a pine-cone instead of a chestnut-burr. They are becoming alike.
evidence: They are all overlapping now, instead of lying side by side.
you're growing to look rather more like a pine-cone, and less like a chestnut-burr,

questions.prompt: Each friend says the other’s hard trick is “so easy.” Is it? Why might they say so?
facilitatorNotes: It is not easy: the Tortoise strains until he goes “black in the face” and grunts. Saying “so easy” may be encouragement, or friendly teasing; readers can decide.
evidence: It's making you black in the face.
which you say is so easy.

readings.title: The Beginning of the Armadillos — two new animals (part 4)
readings.challenge: Find how a rhyme from earlier has been turned around, and judge a mother’s rule.
readings.focus: The friends turn the Jaguar’s rule against him, and become a new animal.
readings.context: Recap: to beat Painted Jaguar’s rhyme (“Can’t curl, but can swim, Slow-Solid, that’s him!”), Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog learned to swim and Slow-Solid Tortoise learned to curl. Practising all night, their prickles and plates turned into overlapping scales. Now they go to find the Jaguar. The Don and the Magdalena in the closing verse were steamships sailing from Southampton, England, to Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented animal-origin story, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Beginning of the Armadillos,” from the meeting with the Jaguar to the end of the story, with the verse “I've never sailed the Amazon”; opens “By and by they found Painted Jaguar, still nursing his paddy-paw that had been hurt the…”; closes “…to Rio— Roll really down to Rio! Oh, I'd love to roll to Rio Some day before I'm old!”.

questions.prompt: How does the Jaguar react when he sees them? Why doesn’t he recognize them?
facilitatorNotes: He is so astonished he falls backward over his tail three times. They no longer look like a hedgehog and a tortoise; both are scaly.
evidence: He was so astonished that he fell three times backward over his own painted tail without stopping.

questions.prompt: Stickly-Prickly recites the Jaguar’s own rhyme, with a change. What has changed, and why is it now true?
facilitatorNotes: The names have swapped: now Stickly-Prickly can swim and Slow-Solid can curl. The rhyme stayed the same; the animals changed.
evidence: Can't curl, but can swim— Stickly-Prickly, that's him!

questions.prompt: Mother Jaguar says “a Hedgehog is a Hedgehog, and can't be anything but a Hedgehog.” Is she right in this story?
facilitatorNotes: No: the friends changed by practice and help. But her other advice, to call it “Armadillo” and leave it alone, is wise. Readers can weigh which part of her answer is right.
evidence: a Hedgehog is a Hedgehog, and can't be anything but a Hedgehog;
And I should leave it alone.

questions.prompt: The narrator says they were called Armadillos “because they were so clever.” What was clever about what they did? What does the verse at the end wish for?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of hiding, each learned the other’s way of staying safe, and turned the Jaguar’s rule upside down. In the verse Kipling says he has never been to Brazil or seen a jaguar or an armadillo, and wishes he could sail to Rio before he is old.
evidence: are always called Armadillos, because they were so clever.
I've never seen a Jaguar,

readings.title: How the First Letter Was Written, part 1: A broken spear
readings.challenge: Enjoy the long joke-names, and notice why Taffy and the Stranger-man cannot understand each other.
readings.focus: A girl and her father need a message sent home, but nobody can write yet.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. This story is not about an animal: it imagines how writing began. Neolithic means from the New Stone Age, thousands of years ago, before writing; a Primitive here is a Stone Age person. Jutes and Angles were early peoples of England; Dravidians are peoples of southern India. Carp are fish; sinews are tough cords from an animal’s body, used for tying; resin is sticky tree gum. “A pretty kettle of fish” means a mess. Slang is very casual language.
readings.contentNote: Taffy’s long name says she ought to be spanked; it is a family joke in the story.

excerpt.locator: “How the First Letter Was Written,” from the beginning to Taffy asking the Stranger-man to fetch the black-handled spear; opens “ONCE upon a most early time was a Neolithic man. He was not a Jute or an Angle, or even a…”; closes “…ask for Daddy's other spear—the one with the black handle that hangs over our fireplace.'”.

questions.prompt: What do the family’s long names mean? Which one do you like best, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Tegumai is “Man-who-does-not-put-his-foot-forward-in-a-hurry,” Teshumai “Lady-who-asks-a-very-many-questions,” and Taffy “Small-person-without-any-manners-who-ought-to-be-spanked.” Each name is a joke about the person. Readers can invent a name like this for themselves.
evidence: 'Man-who-does-not-put-his-foot-forward-in-a-hurry';
'Lady-who-asks-a-very-many-questions';

questions.prompt: What goes wrong at the river, and why can’t Taffy run home for the other spear?
facilitatorNotes: Tegumai breaks his spear on the river bottom, and they are miles from home. He says it is too far for her “little fat legs” and she might fall into the beaver-swamp.
evidence: he accidentally broke it clean across by jabbing it down too hard on the bottom of the river.
'It's too far for your little fat legs,' said Tegumai.

questions.prompt: What does Taffy wish she and her Daddy could do?
facilitatorNotes: Write, so they could send a message home for the new spear. Her father scolds her for saying “awful,” but agrees it would be a convenience.
evidence: 'I say, Daddy, it's an awful nuisance that you and I don't know how to write, isn't it?
If we did we could send a message for the new spear.'

questions.prompt: The Stranger-man thinks Taffy is “a very wonderful child” and her father a great Chief. Why does he think that? What is really happening?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot understand their language, so he guesses from what he sees: a child who stamps and makes faces, and a man who will not look at him must be very important. Really Tegumai is just busy mending his spear. The joke is that both sides misunderstand; ask readers to predict where that will lead.
evidence: She must be the daughter of that noble Chief who is so great that he won't take any notice of me.
and he did not understand one word of Tegumai's language.

readings.title: How the First Letter Was Written, part 2: Taffy’s picture
readings.challenge: Imagine Taffy’s picture from her words, and compare what she means with what the Stranger-man thinks it means.
readings.focus: Taffy draws a message, and the Stranger-man reads it completely wrong.
readings.context: Recap: long ago, before anyone could write, a Stone Age man called Tegumai broke his fish-spear far from home. His daughter Taffy wished they could send a message to her Mummy for the black-handled spear. A Stranger-man came by who spoke a different language; Taffy asked him to fetch the spear, but he understood nothing, and decided Tegumai must be a great Chief. In the printed book a picture of Taffy’s drawing appears where the story says “Now this is the picture”; here, Taffy’s own words describe it. To be ’fended is to be offended.

excerpt.locator: “How the First Letter Was Written,” from the Stranger-man giving Taffy the birch-bark to Tegumai going on fishing; opens “The Stranger-man (and he was a Tewara) thought, 'This is a very, very wonderful child.…”; closes “'Very well,' said Tegumai, and went on fishing.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Stranger-man give Taffy a piece of birch-bark? What does Taffy think it means?
facilitatorNotes: He means it as a sign that his heart is white like the bark and he means no harm. Taffy thinks he wants her Mummy’s address written down. Already they mean different things.
evidence: to show that his heart was as white as the birch-bark and that he meant no harm;
You want my Mummy's living address?

questions.prompt: Why is the Stranger-man surprised when Taffy takes his shark’s tooth?
facilitatorNotes: He was told that anyone who touched his magic tooth without leave would swell up or burst, and she does not. So he decides to be even more polite.
evidence: if anybody touched it without my leave they would immediately swell up or burst,

questions.prompt: List what Taffy draws, and one thing in her picture that does not look the way she meant.
facilitatorNotes: Daddy fishing with the broken spear, the black-handled spear, herself explaining, the Stranger-man holding the spear, two trees, a hill, the beavers’ heads in the swamp, the Cave, and Mummy holding up her hands. The spear looks as if it is “sticking in Daddy's back,” and her hair seems to stand up. Try drawing the picture from her description.
evidence: It looks as if it was sticking in Daddy's back,
I haven't put in all the beavers, because I can't draw beavers, but I've drawn their heads,

questions.prompt: What does the Stranger-man think the picture says? Why do his ideas make sense to him?
facilitatorNotes: That the great Chief is surrounded by enemies with spears and needs his tribe; that is why the Chief turned his back, so hidden enemies would not see a message. Each wrong guess fits what he has seen. Ask readers why a picture can mean different things to different people.
evidence: If I do not fetch this great Chief's tribe to help him, he will be slain by his enemies
Now I see why the great Chief pretended not to notice me!

readings.title: How the First Letter Was Written, part 3: The whole Tribe comes
readings.challenge: Follow a misunderstanding as it grows bigger and bigger, and enjoy Kipling’s heaps of long words.
readings.focus: Taffy’s mother reads the picture as a story of attack, and the whole Tribe marches out.
readings.context: Recap: long ago, before writing, a Stone Age girl called Taffy drew a picture on birch-bark so that a Stranger-man, who did not speak her language, could fetch her father’s other spear from her mother. He thought the picture showed her father, a great Chief, attacked by enemies, and raced off to get help. Kipling piles up grand titles from many countries and times (Hetmans, Neguses, Woons, Akhoonds, Warlocks, Angekoks, Juju-men, Bonzes) for fun; they all mean chiefs, officers or holy men. Villeins and serfs were poor farm workers who served a lord; hierarchical order means arranged from most to least important. An oration is a speech.
readings.contentNote: The Neolithic ladies knock the Stranger-man down, sit on him, pull his hair and fill it with mud, and the Tribe plans to cut off his head; it is played for comedy, and no one is hurt in the end.

excerpt.locator: “How the First Letter Was Written,” from the Stranger-man handing Teshumai the picture to Tegumai saying his only visitor was the Stranger-man; opens “The Stranger-man—did you know he was a Tewara?—hurried away with the picture and ran for…”; closes “…that you are trying to choke. Aren't you well, or are you ill, O Tribe of Tegumai?'”.

questions.prompt: What does Teshumai think the picture shows? Find two things she reads wrong.
facilitatorNotes: That the Stranger-man has stuck Tegumai “all full of spears” and frightened Taffy. The broken spear looks like a broken arm, the spear looks stuck in his back, and the beavers look like “a whole pack of people.”
evidence: He has stuck my Tegumai all full of spears,
they were Taffy's beavers really, but they did look rather like people

questions.prompt: What do the Neolithic ladies do to the Stranger-man? How does he behave?
facilitatorNotes: They knock him down, sit on him in a line of six, fill his hair with mud and call him names. He stays polite and says nothing, though he is “really annoyed.”
evidence: knocked him down and sat on him in a long line of six,
the Stranger-man (in spite of being a Tewara) was really annoyed.

questions.prompt: Kipling lists the whole Tribe marching out, then asks, “Aren’t those beautiful words, Best Beloved?” Read the list aloud. Why might he enjoy them, and do you?
facilitatorNotes: The words are grand, strange and fun to say, and the huge parade is funny because it is all for a broken spear. Some readers love the sound; others find it a jumble. Either answer is fine with a reason.
evidence: (Aren't those beautiful words, Best Beloved?)
they frightened every fish for twenty miles,

questions.prompt: Taffy calls it her “surprise.” Who is most surprised, and why is Tegumai not pleased?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone is surprised: Taffy at the crowd, the Tribe to find Tegumai safe, Teshumai to find no enemies. Tegumai says it “has ruined all my fishing for the day” and calls the Tribe “very interfering.” Readers may choose a different person and explain.
evidence: 'Very,' said Tegumai; 'but it has ruined all my fishing for the day.
You're a very interfering people.'

readings.title: How the First Letter Was Written, part 4: A great invention
readings.challenge: Listen to Taffy explain her picture, then hear what the Head Chief says it means for the future.
readings.focus: A mix-up becomes the first step toward writing, and Kipling ends with a poem about the place where it happened.
readings.context: Recap: long ago, before writing, a Stone Age girl called Taffy drew a picture to send a Stranger-man for her father’s spear. Her mother and the whole Tribe read it as a picture of her father attacked by enemies; they beat the Stranger-man, filled his hair with mud, and marched to the river, only to find Taffy and her father, Tegumai, quite safe. In the verse, Merrow Down, Guildford, the river Wey, Shere, Bramley and Shamley are real places near the town of Guildford in Surrey, in the south of England. The ancient Britons lived there long ago; the Phoenicians were traders from the eastern Mediterranean; to barter is to trade; jet is a black stone; torques are neck rings. “Racial talks” in Kipling’s day meant talks between different peoples.

excerpt.locator: “How the First Letter Was Written,” from the Head Chief’s complaint about the picture to the end of the story and its verse; opens “'He came with a horrible picture,' said the Head Chief,—'a picture that showed you were…”; closes “…than six times bigger then; And all the Tribe of Tegumai They cut a noble figure then!”.

questions.prompt: How does Taffy explain the parts of her picture that frightened everyone?
facilitatorNotes: There was only one spear, drawn three times to make sure; it only looked stuck in Daddy because the bark was too small; the “bad people” were her beavers, showing the way through the swamp; and Mummy looked pleased. Then she calls them “the stupidest people in the world.”
evidence: There was only one spear. I drawded it three times to make sure.
and those things that Mummy called bad people are my beavers.

questions.prompt: Who laughs, and who does not? Why might the ladies not join in?
facilitatorNotes: The Head Chief, the Stranger-man, Tegumai and all the Tribe laugh; Teshumai and the Neolithic ladies do not, and keep saying “idiot!” Perhaps they feel foolish, or are cross that the men are laughing at what they did. Readers may have other ideas.
evidence: The only people who did not laugh were Teshumai Tewindrow and all the Neolithic ladies.
and said 'idiot!' ever so often.

questions.prompt: What does the Head Chief say Taffy has invented? What does he promise about letters, and what advice does he give for next time?
facilitatorNotes: Writing: at present only pictures, which are not always understood, but one day there will be twenty-six letters and people will “say exactly what we mean without any mistakes.” Next time, send someone who speaks their language to explain. Ask whether writing has really ended all mistakes.
evidence: It is a great invention, and some day men will call it writing.
pictures are not always properly understood.

questions.prompt: The verse says the place where Taffy lived is now “A grassy track to-day.” How does the poem change the feeling of the story at the end?
facilitatorNotes: After the comedy, it looks back across thousands of years: bison once roamed there, the river was six times bigger, and the Tribe of Tegumai “cut a noble figure then,” but now there is only a track. Some readers find it a little sad; others find it exciting to imagine people long ago in a real place.
evidence: A grassy track to-day it is—
They cut a noble figure then!

readings.title: How the Alphabet Was Made, part 1: The carp-fish mouth
readings.challenge: Follow how a sound becomes a picture, and draw the sign yourself.
readings.focus: Taffy and her father turn the sound “ah” into a drawing they can both remember.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how an animal came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. This story follows “How the First Letter Was Written,” in which Taffy’s picture-letter was badly misread and a Stranger-man got mud in his hair. Like that story, it is not about an animal: it imagines how the alphabet began. Taffy’s family lives in the Stone Age, before writing. Kipling drew each sign the characters make; the numbers in brackets, such as (1.), point to those drawings, which are not included here, so draw each sign yourself as the characters describe it. Hides are animal skins; a marrow-bone has soft marrow inside to eat; “inciting” is Taffy’s word for exciting. A carp’s feeler is a whisker by its mouth.

excerpt.locator: “How the Alphabet Was Made,” from the beginning to Tegumai promising to be surprised by the carp-fish sign; opens “THE week after Taffimai Metallumai (we will still call her Taffy, Best Beloved) made that…”; closes “…when I see it anywhere, as if you had jumped out from behind a tree and said "Ah!"'”.

questions.prompt: What did the picture-letter mix-up cost Taffy’s Daddy? Who does Taffy say was to blame?
facilitatorNotes: Two soft, fringed deerskins paid to the Stranger-man. Taffy says “We didn't do anything”: it was Mummy, the other ladies, and the mud. Her Daddy would rather not talk about it.
evidence: I had to pay two deerskins—soft ones with fringes—to the Stranger-man
'We didn't do anything,' said Taffy.

questions.prompt: Why does Taffy say her Daddy looks like a carp-fish? Is she being rude?
facilitatorNotes: When he says “Ah!” with his mouth open, he looks like a carp with its mouth open. She says it is not rude but part of her “secret-surprise-think.”
evidence: 'You look just like a carp-fish with its mouth open.
'I'm not meaning rude, really and truly,' said Taffy.

questions.prompt: What will the carp-mouth picture remind Tegumai of? Why does he add the feeler?
facilitatorNotes: The “ah” noise, as if Taffy had jumped out and surprised him. The feeler shows it is a carp, since perch and trout have none.
evidence: it will remind you of that ah-noise.
'cause the perches and trouts haven't got feelers.

questions.prompt: Tegumai speaks “in the voice that grown-ups use when they are truly attending.” What makes him start listening properly? Draw the carp’s open mouth standing on its head, with the feeler across it: what letter does it look like?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that a picture can stand for a sound, not just a thing, and that is something new. Kipling’s drawing looks like the letter A. (The real letter A grew from an old picture of an ox’s head; Kipling’s carp is his own joke.)
evidence: in the voice that grown-ups use when they are truly attending.
Here's just his mouth, and that means ah.

readings.title: How the Alphabet Was Made, part 2: Tail, egg and snake
readings.challenge: Match each new sound to its picture and say why the picture fits.
readings.focus: Signs for sounds can be joined into words, and words can be left for someone far away.
readings.context: Recap: a week after the picture-letter mix-up, Taffy and her father Tegumai, a Stone Age family who cannot write, are fishing by the Wagai river. Taffy has invented a game: a carp-fish’s open mouth, with its feeler across, stands for the sound “ah.” Kipling drew each sign the characters make; the numbers in brackets, such as (1.), point to those drawings, which are not included here, so draw each sign yourself as the characters describe it. Flints are sharp stones once used for spear-heads; fever is an illness with a high temperature.

excerpt.locator: “How the Alphabet Was Made,” from Taffy asking for another noise to her dancing round her Daddy over “yo, bad water”; opens “'Now, make another noise,' said Taffy, very proud.”; closes “…and a round egg! O Daddy, we must tell Mummy, quick!' and Taffy danced all round him.”.

questions.prompt: How do they draw “Yah”? Why does Taffy want the two parts drawn separately?
facilitatorNotes: The “yer” part is a carp’s tail, the “ah” part its mouth. If they are joined she will forget which is which, and a carp standing on its head shows its tail first.
evidence: Draw it separate. Draw his tail.
'Here's a carp-fish tail for the yer-noise.'

questions.prompt: What pictures do they choose for “Oh!” and “Ssh!”? Why do they fit?
facilitatorNotes: An egg or round stone for “Oh,” because the mouth makes a round shape; a hissing snake for “Ssh,” the noise a snake makes when it does not want to be disturbed.
evidence: You make your mouth all around like an egg or a stone.
It's the noise a snake makes, Daddy, when it is thinking and doesn't want to be disturbed.

questions.prompt: Tegumai says they have found “the big secret of the world.” What does he compare it to?
facilitatorNotes: The finest thing since the Tribe began using shark’s teeth instead of flints for spear-heads: a great invention.
evidence: I believe we've found out the big secret of the world.
since the Tribe of Tegumai took to using shark's teeth instead of flints for their spear-heads.

questions.prompt: Tail and egg by a swamp pool spell “yo,” bad water. Why does Taffy dance? What can writing do that talking cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Her Daddy could warn her even when he is miles away hunting; the sign speaks for him. Writing carries words across distance and time. Readers can name signs and notes that do this today.
evidence: 'But I needn't be near the water at all. I might be miles away, hunting, and still——'
All that in a carp-fish-tail and a round egg!

readings.title: How the Alphabet Was Made, part 3: Sky-water
readings.challenge: Find the problem each new sign solves, and read a word the way Taffy does.
readings.focus: Signs must not be mixed up, and Taffy reads her first word without being told it.
readings.context: Recap: Taffy and her father Tegumai, Stone Age people who cannot yet write, are inventing signs for sounds: a carp-fish’s open mouth for “ah,” its tail for “yer,” an egg for “oh,” a snake for “ssh.” They have found that tail and egg by a pool can say “yo,” bad water, even when Tegumai is far away. Drying-poles are frames for hanging animal skins to dry. Kipling drew each sign the characters make; the numbers in brackets, such as (1.), point to those drawings, which are not included here, so draw each sign yourself as the characters describe it.

excerpt.locator: “How the Alphabet Was Made,” from “so,” dinner, and “sho,” the drying-poles, to Taffy reading “shu-ya” as the rain begins; opens “'Not yet,' said Tegumai; 'not till we've gone a little further. Let's see. Yo is bad…”; closes “…know it was going to rain and I'd take my beaver-skin hood. Wouldn't Mummy be surprised!'”.

questions.prompt: What problem does Tegumai see with the snake-and-egg sign? Why does it matter so much to Taffy?
facilitatorNotes: “So” means dinner but “sho” means the drying-poles. If Taffy came home for dinner and found she had to hang hot, hairy hides, she would be cross.
evidence: So means "come and have dinner," but sho means the drying-poles
I hate helping to hang heavy, hot, hairy hides on them.

questions.prompt: Why does Taffy reject the spotty snake, and what do they draw instead?
facilitatorNotes: Spots might be left out in a hurry and she would be caught. They draw the drying-poles themselves after the snake, “and make quite sure.”
evidence: And p'raps if you were in a hurry you might leave them out,
I think we'd better draw a picture of the horrid high drying-poles their very selves,

questions.prompt: How do they show the thin “oo” sound? Why not a thin egg?
facilitatorNotes: A round egg with a little hole at the end, “to show how the O-noise runs out all thin.” A thin egg drawn in a hurry might be mistaken for the round one.
evidence: We'll open a little hole at the end of the round egg to show how the O-noise runs out all thin,
If we drew that in a hurry we might mistake it for the round egg itself.

questions.prompt: Taffy reads “shu-ya” just as a raindrop falls. Why is this the moment they have “found the Secret”?
facilitatorNotes: She worked out a message nobody said aloud: “I told it you without saying a word.” The raindrop proves she read it right. Some readers may say the raindrop helped her guess; Taffy admits it “made me quite sure.”
evidence: If you can, we've found the Secret.'
'And I told it you without saying a word, didn't I?'

readings.title: How the Alphabet Was Made, part 4: “Shu-ya-las ya-maru”
readings.challenge: Build a whole sentence sound by sound, and notice the little inventions that make it readable.
readings.focus: Father and daughter write their first sentence, with signs as simple as they can make them and spaces between words.
readings.context: Recap: Taffy and her father Tegumai, a Stone Age family who cannot write, have invented signs for sounds (a carp’s open mouth, its tail, an egg, a snake, drying-poles, an egg with a hole), and Taffy has just read their first written word, “shu-ya,” sky-water, rain. In their language “las” means ending or breaking and “maru” means come to. Kipling drew each sign the characters make; the numbers in brackets, such as (1.), point to those drawings, which are not included here, so draw each sign yourself as the characters describe it. To jostle is to bump and push.

excerpt.locator: “How the Alphabet Was Made,” from Tegumai dancing to his saying “That's enough for to-day”; opens “Tegumai got up and danced. (Daddies didn't mind doing those things in those days.) 'More…”; closes “…for years and years after the biggest trees you can see are all chopped up for firewood.'”.

questions.prompt: What message does Tegumai want to write next? Why is it so hard?
facilitatorNotes: “Shu-ya-las, ya maru”: the rain is ending, come to the river. It needs new sounds, like la, m and r, and they are “the first people in all the world” to try.
evidence: 'Shu-ya-las, ya maru. (Sky-water ending. River come to.)
And we're the first people in all the world who've ever tried to do it, Taffimai!'

questions.prompt: How do they find a sign for “la”? What does Taffy wish she had drawn for the Stranger-man?
facilitatorNotes: “Las” also means breaking, and “shi-las” means a broken spear, so a broken spear becomes “la.” She wishes she had written “shi-las” instead of “silly beaver pictures.”
evidence: 'And shi-las means that your spear is broken.
If I'd only thought of that instead of drawing silly beaver pictures for the Stranger!'

questions.prompt: What pictures do they make for “m” and for “rrr”? Why does Tegumai put in only one tooth?
facilitatorNotes: A shut mouth for “m”; the rough edge of a shark-tooth saw for “rrr.” He keeps it simple: “the easier we make our sound-pictures the better for everybody.”
evidence: We'll draw a shut mouth like this.'
the easier we make our sound-pictures the better for everybody.

questions.prompt: Taffy suggests putting something between the words so they won’t “jostle.” Why is that a good idea? Try writing a sentence with no spaces and see.
facilitatorNotes: Without spaces, the signs run together and are hard to read, “same as if they were carps.” Tegumai leaves a space: the first space between words. Readers will find a no-space sentence slow and confusing.
evidence: Hadn't we better put a little bit of stick or something between each word,
'Oh, I'll leave a space for that,' said her Daddy.

readings.title: How the Alphabet Was Made, part 5: The Alphabet, all complete
readings.challenge: Follow how pictures turned into plain letters, then listen to how the closing verse changes the mood.
readings.focus: Drawn over and over, the sound-pictures grow simpler until they are an alphabet; the verse remembers Taffy long ago.
readings.context: Recap: Taffy and her father Tegumai, a Stone Age family, have spent a day inventing a sign for each sound (a carp’s mouth, a tail, an egg, a snake, drying-poles, a broken spear, a shut mouth, a saw-tooth) and have written their first sentence, about rain and the river. They are keeping it a secret from Taffy’s mother, Teshumai. A water-tank here is a stone basin for water; a pike is a fierce fish. Hieroglyphics, Demotics, Runics and Cufics are real kinds of old writing; Kipling mixes in made-up ones for fun. Surrey is a county in the south of England, where the first story’s verse places Taffy’s home; bracken is fern; elf-locks are tangled curls.
readings.contentNote: Kipling’s daughter Josephine, for whom he first told the Taffy stories, died in 1899 at the age of six; many readers hear that loss in the closing verse.

excerpt.locator: “How the Alphabet Was Made,” from the evening of drawing by the fire to the end of the story and its verse; opens “So they went home, and all that evening Tegumai sat on one side of the fire and Taffy on…”; closes “…far she cannot call to him, Comes Tegumai alone to find The daughter that was all to him.”.

questions.prompt: What message does Taffy find on the water-tank? What does she do, and what does she think of writing now?
facilitatorNotes: “Ya-las”: the water is running out. She fills the tank, and grumbles, “These picture-sounds are rather a bother!” Writing can also give you chores. Then she pulls her Daddy’s ear, the one she may pull when she has been good.
evidence: she saw Ya-las (water is ending or running out) chalked on the side of the big stone water-tank,
'These picture-sounds are rather a bother!

questions.prompt: How did the T-sound picture change? Why did all the pictures become plainer?
facilitatorNotes: It began as the whole family holding hands; drawn six or seven times it got scratchier, until it was only a thin, long Tegumai with his arms out. Drawn over and over, every picture became “plainer and easier.”
evidence: till at last the T-sound was only a thin long Tegumai with his arms out
they became plainer and easier,

questions.prompt: Choose two other letters from Kipling’s list and explain where he says their shapes came from. Is this how the alphabet really began?
facilitatorNotes: Z is the snake turned round; E a twiddle; B the beaver; N noses; G a pike’s mouth; K the pike’s mouth with a spear; W the winding river. It is Kipling’s invention; the real alphabet grew over thousands of years from old picture-signs, as the story hints with “thousands and thousands” of years.
evidence: They turned the hissy-snake the other way round for the Z-sound,
and there was the Alphabet, all complete.

questions.prompt: In the verse, Taffy comes “dancing through the fern,” but Tegumai comes “alone” and “so far she cannot call to him.” How does the ending feel after the jokes of the story? Why might Kipling end this way?
facilitatorNotes: Many readers find it sad and full of longing: the Tribe is gone, and a father searches for “The daughter that was all to him.” Knowing about Kipling’s daughter makes it sadder; some readers see it simply as a picture of the far past. Let readers say how it made them feel, gently.
evidence: Comes Taffy dancing through the fern
The daughter that was all to him.

readings.title: The Crab That Played with the Sea, part 1: The play of the Very Beginning
readings.challenge: Follow the Magician’s journey North, East, West and South, and keep track of the one animal who slipped away.
readings.focus: In a made-up story of the world’s beginning, every animal is given its play except one, who runs off.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how something came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. This story explains the tides, the daily rising and falling of the sea, in a made-up way. It is set in Malaya (now part of Malaysia): the Perak is a real river there, and Selangor, Malacca, Singapore and Bingtang are real places. “Kun?” means “Is this right?” and “Payah kun” means “That is quite right”; the story tells you so. “Son of Adam” means a human being. A kris is a Malay dagger. Keep a map or globe nearby: the story keeps saying “you can look them out on the map.”
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about the tides, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Crab That Played with the Sea,” from the beginning to the canoe being pulled out to sea, ending “as though it had been pulled by a string”; opens “BEFORE the High and Far-Off Times, O my Best Beloved, came the Time of the Very…”; closes “…out and out to the Island of Bingtang, as though it had been pulled by a string.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Eldest Magician tell each animal to do? Why does he call it a “play”?
facilitatorNotes: He tells each one to “Play at being” itself: the Elephant at being an Elephant, the Beaver at being a Beaver. Each animal’s way of living is its play, a game it was taught. Ask what the Turtle’s play would look like.
evidence: Play at being an Elephant,
One by one he took all the beasts and birds and fishes and told them what to play at.

questions.prompt: Who saw Pau Amma the Crab slip away, and why did nobody else notice?
facilitatorNotes: Only the Man’s little daughter, leaning on his shoulder. The Magician and the Man were busy talking. Tell readers to remember this; it will matter later.
evidence: Nobody saw him go away except the little girl-daughter where she leaned on the Man's shoulder.
Now, while the two were talking together,

questions.prompt: The Magician visits four animals. What happens the same way each time, and what is different?
facilitatorNotes: Each animal asks “Kun?”, he answers “Payah kun,” and he breathes on what it has done so that it becomes a real place: the Himalayas, the Indian Desert and the Sahara, the Everglades, the Malay islands. The pattern is easy to remember, and listeners can join in.
evidence: and they became the great Himalayan Mountains, and you can look them out on the map.
they became the Everglades in Florida,

questions.prompt: When the Magician says the Man is too wise for the play, what does the Man answer? What does he want?
facilitatorNotes: He agrees, and asks that all the Animals be made obedient to him: he wants to be in charge, not to play. Some readers find him proud, others practical. Point out that the Crab escapes while he is talking.
evidence: Yes, I am too wise for this play; but see that you make all the Animals obedient to me.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the Sea, according to the Man? Why does the Magician call it “a new and a bad play”?
facilitatorNotes: Twice a day it floods up the river into his house, and twice a day it drains away, leaving mud and upsetting his canoe. Nobody was taught that play, so someone is playing a game of his own. Readers who know about tides may guess what the story is explaining.
evidence: Once a day and once a night the Sea runs up the Perak river
That is a new and a bad play.

readings.title: The Crab That Played with the Sea, part 2: Who is playing with the Sea?
readings.challenge: Draw an animal from a description before you are told its name, and explain a made-up cause of the tides.
readings.focus: A child who noticed something at the beginning solves the mystery.
readings.context: Recap: at the Very Beginning the Eldest Magician taught every animal its play, but Pau Amma the Crab slipped into the sea while the Man was talking, and only the Man’s little daughter saw him go. Now the Sea floods the Man’s house twice a day and drains away twice a day, and a strong current has pulled the Magician, the Man and the girl far out to sea in a canoe. Hunchbacked means bent over with a curved back. The Fisher of the Moon and the Rat of the Moon are Kipling’s inventions, like the shapes people have long imagined in the moon’s face. Pusat Tasek means “the Heart of the Sea”; Pauh Janggi is a magic tree of Malay legend; Raja means king.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about the tides, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Crab That Played with the Sea,” from the Magician calling the beasts, birds and fishes to Pau Amma being dared to come up and talk; opens “Then the Eldest Magician stood up and shouted, 'Ho! beasts, birds, and fishes, that I…”; closes “…me at the Very Beginning; but if you are not afraid, come up and we will talk about it.'”.

questions.prompt: The Magician asks the beasts, the Fisher of the Moon and the Rat. What does each answer? Why will the Fisherman and the Rat never finish?
facilitatorNotes: None of them plays with the Sea. The Fisherman spins a line to catch the world, and the Rat bites through it as fast as it is made, so neither job can ever be done. It is a funny, endless pair of chores.
evidence: I am spinning a line with which I shall some day catch the world;
I am too busy biting through the line that this old Fisherman is spinning.

questions.prompt: How does the girl describe the animal that ran away? Draw it from her words. What is it?
facilitatorNotes: Round and flat, eyes on stalks, walking sideways, armour on its back: a crab. Kipling lets her describe it before the Magician names it.
evidence: He was round and he was flat; and his eyes grew upon stalks; and he walked sideways like this;

questions.prompt: The Magician says “How wise are little children who see and are silent!” and then “How wise are little children who speak truth!” Can both be wise? When should she keep quiet, and when should she speak?
facilitatorNotes: She was wise to watch quietly, and wise to speak now that it helps. Some readers think she should have told at once; Pau Amma himself will say so later. Others think she could not have known it mattered. Accept either with a reason.
evidence: How wise are little children who see and are silent!
How wise are little children who speak truth!

questions.prompt: How does the story explain the sea going out and coming in? Use the words about the basin.
facilitatorNotes: When Pau Amma leaves his hollow, the sea pours down into it and the beaches are left bare; when he sits in it, the water rises, as it does when you put your hand into a basin. Try it with a bowl of water. This is the story’s made-up cause; the Moon’s part comes later.
evidence: all the Sea rose up as water rises in a basin when you put your hand into it.
all the beaches of all the islands are left bare,

questions.prompt: What does Pau Amma say when he learns what his coming and going does? What does his answer show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He laughs, says he did not know he was so important, and threatens to go out seven times a day. He enjoys his power more than he cares about the little fish and the drowned islands. Ask what a kinder answer would have been.
evidence: I did not know I was so important.
Henceforward I will go out seven times a day, and the waters shall never be still.

readings.title: The Crab That Played with the Sea, part 3: Soft as a little crab
readings.challenge: Explain a character’s problem in his own words, and judge whether his complaints are fair.
readings.focus: A proud giant is made small and soft, and has to choose what kind of crab to be.
readings.context: Recap: Pau Amma the Crab escaped the Eldest Magician at the Very Beginning, and now he makes the Sea flood and drain twice a day by going out of his hollow, Pusat Tasek, the Heart of the Sea, and coming back. The Man’s daughter told the Magician who it was, and Pau Amma, proud of his power, has been dared to come up and talk. Sarawak and Pahang are places on two coasts far apart across the sea. A husk is the dry outer covering of a nut; dogfish are small sharks; to lament is to cry out in sorrow. The magic twin nuts grow on the Wonderful Tree.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about the tides, not a scientific explanation.

excerpt.locator: “The Crab That Played with the Sea,” from Pau Amma rising in the moonlight to his choice, ending “I will take all the gifts”; opens “'I am not afraid,' said Pau Amma, and he rose to the top of the sea in the moonlight.…”; closes “…Pau Amma thought a little and said, 'I have made my choice. I will take all the gifts.'”.

questions.prompt: How big is Pau Amma? Find the words that make him seem enormous.
facilitatorNotes: One side of his shell touched the beach at Sarawak and the other the beach at Pahang, and he was taller than the smoke of three volcanoes: the King Crab of all Crabs.
evidence: One side of his great shell touched the beach at Sarawak; the other touched the beach at Pahang;
he was taller than the smoke of three volcanoes!

questions.prompt: Pau Amma is asked to make a Magic. What can he do, and what can the Magician do with one little finger?
facilitatorNotes: Pau Amma can only stir up the Sea, because he is “nothing more than a Crab.” With the little finger of his left hand the Magician makes the hard shell fall off. Being huge is not the same as being powerful.
evidence: he could only stir up the Sea,
with just the little finger of his left hand

questions.prompt: Soft and ashamed, Pau Amma is in a terrible fix. Explain his problem in his own words.
facilitatorNotes: Anywhere but his hollow, soft as he is, the sharks and dogfish will eat him; but if he stays in it he can never go out for food, and will die. Either choice is dangerous.
evidence: if I go anywhere else, all soft as I am now, the sharks and the dogfish will eat me.
I can never stir out to get my food, and so I shall die.

questions.prompt: Pau Amma says “I do not choose yet” and blames the Man and the girl. Is that fair?
facilitatorNotes: He says that if the Man had not taken the Magician’s attention, and if the girl had spoken, none of this would have happened. There is something in it, but he chose to run away; he is also bargaining for more gifts. Let readers judge.
evidence: If he had not taken up your attention I should not have grown tired of waiting and run away,
If she had spoken then, the Eldest Magician would have called me back,

questions.prompt: The Magician gives back the shell, but it will go soft for one month every year. Why? Is it a fair bargain?
facilitatorNotes: To remind Pau Amma that the Magician can make magics and to keep him humble; with every gift he might grow too bold and too greedy. Real crabs do shed their shells as they grow and stay soft for a while; Kipling turns that fact into a lesson. Opinions on fairness may differ.
evidence: on the twelfth month of every year it shall grow soft again,
to keep you humble, Pau Amma;

readings.title: The Crab That Played with the Sea, part 4: The Moon’s fishing-line, and a riddle
readings.challenge: Find the true fact hidden in a made-up ending, and enjoy a riddle-poem for its sound.
readings.focus: The story ends by explaining the tides, the crabs we find on beaches, and why crabs nip.
readings.context: Recap: Pau Amma, the giant King Crab who escaped the Eldest Magician at the Very Beginning, has been making the Sea flood and drain by going in and out of his hollow at the Heart of the Sea. The Magician took away his hard shell, and Pau Amma has now chosen all the gifts offered him: safe hiding places under every stone, a home on land and in the sea, and the girl’s scissors. Spring-tides are the highest tides and neap-tides the lowest; they have nothing to do with the season of spring. The poem names steamship companies of Kipling’s day by initials and nicknames (P. and O., B.I.); it is a riddle about which ships pass near the crabs’ home. A mangosteen is a tropical fruit; the Times was a London newspaper that printed news of ships. Read the poem for its bouncing sound; nobody needs to know the ships.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about the tides, not a scientific explanation. Kipling makes a pun on the name of the Malay people, calling them “the Malazy—the lazy people.” That was an unfair stereotype that British writers of his time often repeated about the peoples Britain ruled; it is not true of Malay people.

excerpt.locator: “The Crab That Played with the Sea,” from Pau Amma growing small to the end, with the closing verses and the note about the shipping page; opens “Then the Eldest Magician made a Magic with the right hand, with all five fingers of his…”; closes “…ought to be able to do that; but if you can't read, ask some one to show it you.”.

questions.prompt: What does little Pau Amma say once he has the scissors? How have the words “I did not know I was so important” changed since he said them before?
facilitatorNotes: He lists everything he can now do. Before, the words meant he was proud of making floods; now he is tiny but delighted with useful gifts. The same words carry a new feeling.
evidence: I can eat nuts. I can crack shells. I can dig holes. I can climb trees.
I did not know I was so important. Kun?

questions.prompt: The Man grumbles about paddling home. How does he turn the Magician’s scolding into a good bargain?
facilitatorNotes: Called lazy, he asks that the Sea work for him twice a day for ever, so boats are carried in and out. The Magician laughs and agrees. Some readers find him clever; others think he got away with it. Discuss the content note about the “Malazy” pun here: Kipling’s joke is unfair to a real people.
evidence: If I am to be lazy all my days, let the Sea work for me twice a day for ever. That will save paddling.

questions.prompt: According to the story, what makes the tides now? What are spring-tides and neap-tides?
facilitatorNotes: The Fisher of the Moon pulls the sea with his line: too hard makes spring-tides, too softly makes neap-tides. Scientists agree that the Moon’s pull causes tides, though not with a fishing-line, so Kipling hides a true fact inside his made-up story.
evidence: From that day to this the Moon has always pulled the sea up and down and made what we call the tides.
Sometimes the Fisher of the Sea pulls a little too hard, and then we get spring-tides;

questions.prompt: What does the narrator say about Pau Amma’s babies? Why does he say it “isn’t fair” to hunt them?
facilitatorNotes: They hide under stones and weed, wave their scissors, sometimes climb palm trees, and shed their armour once a year. It isn’t fair to punish them for old Pau Amma’s rudeness, and if you carry them home in a pickle-bottle and they nip you, “it serves you right!” It is a playful way of saying: leave crabs in peace.
evidence: it isn't fair to kill or hunt Pau Amma's babies just because old Pau Amma was stupidly rude a very long time ago.
That is why they nip you with their scissors, and it serves you right!

questions.prompt: Read the riddle-poem aloud. Which rhymes are surprising or funny? What does the narrator say to do if you cannot wait to solve it?
facilitatorNotes: Rhymes such as “cargoes” and “Lagos,” “try a” and “Sourabaya.” He says to look at the shipping page of the Times and then the Atlas, to see how the steamers’ ports fit the places in the poem, or to ask someone to show you. Kipling loved ships and maps; the riddle is about which ship routes pass near the crabs’ sea.
evidence: To Penang instead of Lagos,
then take the Atlas (and that is the finest picture-book in the world)

readings.title: The Cat That Walked by Himself, part 1: The First Friend
readings.challenge: Hear the repeated phrases and notice how a bargain turns an enemy into a friend.
readings.focus: The Woman makes a home and wins over the Dog, while the Cat watches and keeps his freedom.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how something came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. This story imagines how the wild animals first came to live with people. “By their wild lones” means each one all alone. “Nenni” is an old word for “no.” Fenugreek and coriander are herbs; grenadillas are fruits. A blade-bone is a flat shoulder-bone: long ago people really did look for signs in the marks on such bones, and here the Woman uses one to make her magic.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about how animals came to live with people, not history or science.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from the beginning to Wild Dog being named the First Friend; opens “HEAR and attend and listen; for this befell and behappened and became and was, O my Best…”; closes “…be our friend for always and always and always. Take him with you when you go hunting.'”.

questions.prompt: What does the Woman do with the Cave? How do her changes begin to tame the Man?
facilitatorNotes: She chooses a dry Cave instead of wet leaves, strews clean sand, lights a fire, hangs a horse-skin across the opening and tells him to wipe his feet. Making a home is what starts to tame him; Kipling’s joke is that housekeeping, not fighting, changed the world.
evidence: She picked out a nice dry Cave, instead of a heap of wet leaves, to lie down in;
Wipe your feet, dear, when you come in, and now we'll keep house.

questions.prompt: How does the Woman win Wild Dog? What does each of them promise?
facilitatorNotes: She throws him a roasted bone, and when he asks for another she offers as many bones as he needs if he helps the Man hunt by day and guards the Cave at night. He agrees and lays his head on her lap: food in exchange for work and loyalty.
evidence: help my Man to hunt through the day and guard this Cave at night, and I will give you as many roast bones as you need.

questions.prompt: What does Wild Dog call the Woman before he agrees, and after? Why does it change?
facilitatorNotes: Before: “O my Enemy and Wife of my Enemy.” After: “O my Friend and Wife of my Friend.” The bargain turns enemies into friends, and his new name, the First Friend, says the same.
evidence: O my Enemy and Wife of my Enemy, what is this that smells so good in the Wild Woods?
O my Friend and Wife of my Friend,

questions.prompt: The Cat says “I will not come,” then follows anyway. What does he want? What does he think of the Dog?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to see and hear everything but leave “at my own liking,” keeping his freedom. He calls the Woman wise but not so wise as himself, and the Dog “very foolish.” Was the Dog foolish or sensible? Readers will differ.
evidence: Why should I not go too and see and look and come away at my own liking.
That is a very foolish Dog.

questions.prompt: Find words that Kipling repeats. Why would a story told aloud use so many repeats?
facilitatorNotes: “I am the Cat who walks by himself, and all places are alike to me”; “Wild Thing out of the Wild Woods”; “wild” in nearly every line. Repeats are fun to say together and help listeners remember who is who.
evidence: I am the Cat who walks by himself, and all places are alike to me.
Wild Thing out of the Wild Woods, taste and try.

readings.title: The Cat That Walked by Himself, part 2: The First Servant and the Giver of Good Food
readings.challenge: Compare what each animal gives and gets, and notice how Kipling shortens a pattern the listener already knows.
readings.focus: The Horse and the Cow make their bargains, and the Cat keeps watching.
readings.context: Recap: long ago, when all the animals were wild, the Woman made a home in a dry Cave and began to tame the Man. With a roast bone she won over Wild Dog, who became the First Friend. The Cat, who “walks by himself,” would not come, but followed secretly to listen. New-mown hay is freshly cut grass, dried. A halter is a strap round an animal’s head for leading it; to plait is to braid.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about how animals came to live with people, not history or science.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from the Second Singing Magic to Wild Cow being named the Giver of Good Food; opens “Next night the Woman cut great green armfuls of fresh grass from the water-meadows, and…”; closes “…I will take care of her while you and the First Friend and the First Servant go hunting.'”.

questions.prompt: What does the Woman get ready before Wild Horse comes? How does she seem to know he is coming?
facilitatorNotes: She dries fresh grass by the fire until it smells like hay, plaits a halter, and makes the Second Singing Magic with the blade-bone. When she hears him she laughs, “Here comes the second.” Her magic and the sweet smell seem to draw him.
evidence: dried it before the fire, so that it smelt like new-mown hay,
She made the Second Singing Magic in the world.

questions.prompt: Wild Horse says he came to find Wild Dog. What does the Woman say he really came for? Is she right?
facilitatorNotes: She says he came for the grass, and he admits it at once. She reads his real wish better than he says it.
evidence: you did not come here for Wild Dog, but for the sake of this good grass.
That is true; give it me to eat.

questions.prompt: Wild Dog became a Friend, but Wild Horse becomes a Servant. What is the difference?
facilitatorNotes: The Horse wears a halter and will carry the family from place to place; he promises to be her servant for the grass. A friend chooses to stay close; a servant works for someone. Some readers think the Horse gave up more than the Dog did.
evidence: His name is not Wild Horse any more, but the First Servant,
I will be your servant for the sake of the wonderful grass.

questions.prompt: Kipling tells Wild Cow’s visit very quickly. How does he save time, and why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: He says everything happened “just the same as before,” over and over. Listeners already know the pattern and can fill it in; the repeated “same” becomes the joke.
evidence: and everything happened just the same as before; and the Cat said the same things as before,

questions.prompt: Each time, the Cat “never told anybody.” Why might he keep what he sees a secret?
facilitatorNotes: Possible answers: he is learning the Woman’s ways for himself; he does not care about the other wild animals; he is planning something. The story has not said yet, so ask for a prediction with a reason.
evidence: But he never told anybody.
'Ah,' said the Cat, listening, 'this is a clever Woman, but she is not so clever as I am.'

readings.title: The Cat That Walked by Himself, part 3: The Cat’s bargain
readings.challenge: Explain each step of a bargain, and decide when a character is only pretending.
readings.focus: The Cat, who will be neither friend nor servant, tricks the Woman into a promise she thinks she will never keep.
readings.context: Recap: the Woman has tamed the Man and won over three wild animals: Wild Dog became the First Friend, Wild Horse the First Servant, and Wild Cow the Giver of Good Food, who gives milk.
