Each time the Cat followed secretly, listened, said he walks by himself, and told nobody. “Told tales” means told about someone behind his back.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about how animals came to live with people, not history or science.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from the Cat going to the Cave by himself to the Bat’s news of the Baby, ending “then my time has come”; opens “Next day the Cat waited to see if any other Wild thing would go up to the Cave, but no…”; closes “'Ah,' said the Cat, listening, 'then my time has come.'”.

questions.prompt: The Woman says they need no more friends or servants. How does the Cat answer, and how does she turn his words against him?
facilitatorNotes: He says he is neither friend nor servant but the Cat who walks by himself, and wants to come in. She answers that he has said it himself, so he should go and walk by himself. His proud motto now shuts him out.
evidence: I am not a friend, and I am not a servant.
You have said it yourself.

questions.prompt: How does the Cat change his manner to get a bargain? Which of his words work on the Woman?
facilitatorNotes: He pretends to be sorry, asks sad questions, and calls her very wise and very beautiful. She says she knew she was wise but did not know she was beautiful, so the flattery works. Ask whether the Cat means it.
evidence: Then Cat pretended to be sorry
I knew I was wise, but I did not know I was beautiful.

questions.prompt: Explain the bargain. What does the Cat get for one, two and three words of praise?
facilitatorNotes: One word: he may come into the Cave. Two: he may sit by the fire. Three: he may drink the warm white milk three times a day for ever. She says “I never shall,” so she thinks the promise is safe.
evidence: If ever I say one word in your praise you may come into the Cave.
you may drink the warm white milk three times a day for always and always and always.

questions.prompt: Why does the Cat ask the Curtain, the Fire and the Milk-pots to “remember”? And why doesn’t the Woman tell the Man?
facilitatorNotes: He wants witnesses so the promise will be kept; predict that these things will act later. She keeps the bargain from the Man and the animals because she is afraid they might not like it, so she has a secret too.
evidence: remember what my Enemy and the Wife of my Enemy has said.
because she was afraid that they might not like it.

questions.prompt: What does the Bat tell the Cat, and why does the Cat say “then my time has come”? What might his plan be?
facilitatorNotes: There is a new Baby who loves things that are soft and tickle, warm things to hold, and being played with, which is exactly what a cat is. He plans to win praise through the Baby. Ask readers how.
evidence: He is fond of things that are soft and tickle,
then my time has come.

readings.title: The Cat That Walked by Himself, part 4: A blessing, a purr and a mouse
readings.challenge: Track how each of the Woman’s plans turns into another word of praise.
readings.focus: The Cat wins his first two places, and the Woman’s own magic helps him toward the third.
readings.context: Recap: the Cat, who walks by himself, would not be the Woman’s friend or servant like the Dog, the Horse and the Cow, but he wants the warm Cave, the fire and the milk. He made a bargain: for one word of praise he may come into the Cave, for two sit by the fire, for three drink the milk three times a day. She said she never would praise him. Now the Bat has told him about a new Baby. A spindle-whorl is a small weight used in spinning thread; “at my wits’ end” means not knowing what to do next; a Still Magic is a magic of silence. “Ouh! Chee!” is a cry of disgust.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about how animals came to live with people, not history or science.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from the Cat hiding near the Cave to the Woman thanking him for catching the mouse; opens “Next night Cat walked through the Wet Wild Woods and hid very near the Cave till…”; closes “…Friend is not quick enough to catch little mice as you have done. You must be very wise.'”.

questions.prompt: How does the Cat earn the first word of praise? Did the Woman know she was praising him?
facilitatorNotes: He pats and tickles the crying Baby until it laughs. The Bat reports that a Wild Thing is playing with the Baby, and the Woman says “A blessing on that Wild Thing whoever he may be”—without knowing it is the Cat.
evidence: A blessing on that Wild Thing whoever he may be,
And the Baby laughed;

questions.prompt: What happens each time she praises him? Find Kipling’s sound words.
facilitatorNotes: The horse-skin Curtain falls (“woosh!”), and then the smoke comes down (“puff!”), because each thing “remembered the bargain.” Then the Cat is sitting “quite comfy” in his new place.
evidence: fell down—woosh!—because it remembered the bargain
came down in clouds from the roof—puff!—

questions.prompt: The Woman is angry, yet she helps the Cat the second time. Why? What does he do with the spindle-whorl?
facilitatorNotes: The Baby is crying so hard she is at her wits’ end. The Cat chases the whorl on its thread, rolls and pounces until the Baby laughs, then purrs it to sleep. Real cats chase string; the story turns a real habit into magic.
evidence: because I am at my wits' end; but I will not thank you for it.
till the Baby laughed as loudly as it had been crying,

questions.prompt: The Woman makes a Still Magic so she will not praise the Cat again. How does her own magic help him instead?
facilitatorNotes: The Cave grows so still that a mouse creeps out; she jumps on a footstool, begs the Cat to eat it, and then thanks and praises him. Her plan turns against her. Ask what she might have done instead.
evidence: the Cave grew so still that a little wee-wee mouse crept out of a corner
A hundred thanks. Even the First Friend is not quick enough to catch little mice as you have done.

questions.prompt: Each time he wins, the Cat says “But still I am the Cat who walks by himself.” Why does he keep saying it?
facilitatorNotes: He wants it understood that he got his place by a bargain, not by becoming a friend or servant; he keeps his independence. Some readers find him proud and rude; others admire him.
evidence: But still I am the Cat who walks by himself, and all places are alike to me.

readings.title: The Cat That Walked by Himself, part 5: The Man, the Dog, and Binkie
readings.challenge: Explain how one sentence spoils two bargains, then compare the story’s ending with a poem that takes a side.
readings.focus: The Cat wins the milk but not the Man or the Dog, and stays the Cat who walks by himself.
readings.context: Recap: the Cat would not be the Woman’s friend or servant, but bargained for a place in the Cave: one word of praise to come in, two to sit by the fire, three to drink the milk. By playing with her Baby and purring it to sleep he won two words, and when he caught a mouse that frightened her, she praised him a third time. “Knobby” means lumpy and hard. In the poem, Pussy is a pet cat and Binkie the speaker’s dog; “to ’muse herself” means to amuse herself. Man Friday and Crusoe come from Robinson Crusoe, a story in which a shipwrecked man finds a footprint in the sand; the child wets the cat’s paw to make one.
readings.contentNote: This is an invented story about how animals came to live with people, not history or science. The Man throws his boots and axe at the Cat and the Dog chases him up a tree, and the story says that is why men and dogs still do it. That is Kipling’s joke, not a way to treat cats.

excerpt.locator: “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from the Milk-pot cracking to the end, with the closing verses; opens “That very moment and second, O Best Beloved, the Milk-pot that stood by the fire cracked…”; closes “…only pretend; But Binkie, he snores at my feet all night, And he is my Firstest Friend!”.

questions.prompt: How does the Cat win the milk? What does the Woman say when it happens?
facilitatorNotes: The Milk-pot cracks (“ffft”) and he laps from one piece. She laughs, gives him a bowl, and says he is as clever as a man, but warns that his bargain was not made with the Man or the Dog.
evidence: O Cat, you are as clever as a man, but remember that your bargain was not made with the Man or the Dog,

questions.prompt: What bargains do the Man and the Dog make with the Cat, and what does the Cat promise each of them?
facilitatorNotes: The Man: catch mice, or he will throw five things at him; the Cat promises to catch mice. The Dog: be kind to the Baby, or he will hunt and bite him; the Cat promises kindness as long as the Baby does not pull his tail too hard.
evidence: I will catch mice when I am in the Cave for always and always and always;
as long as he does not pull my tail too hard,

questions.prompt: The Cat agrees to both bargains, yet the Man throws things and the Dog chases him. What did the Cat say that spoiled it?
facilitatorNotes: Each time he adds “But still I am the Cat who walks by himself,” and each answers “If you had not said that last” he would have been at peace with him. His pride costs him their friendship. Was keeping his freedom worth it? Readers may disagree.
evidence: If you had not said that last I would have put all these things away for always and always and always;

questions.prompt: The story ends by telling what cats do “from that day to this.” Which parts match real cats you know?
facilitatorNotes: They catch mice, are kind to babies until their tails are pulled, and go out at night onto roofs and into trees. Kipling invents a reason for real habits. (Throwing things at cats is part of the joke, not something to do.)
evidence: He will kill mice and he will be kind to Babies when he is in the house, just as long as they do not pull his tail too hard.
when the moon gets up and night comes, he is the Cat that walks by himself,

questions.prompt: In the poem, does the speaker love Pussy or Binkie more? What reasons are given? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Binkie, the dog: he behaves, plays whatever the child chooses, and snores at the child’s feet all night, while Pussy plays to amuse herself, won’t attend, and goes out at night, so her love is “only pretend.” The poem takes the side of the First Friend. Cat-lovers may well disagree.
evidence: So I know it is only pretend;
And he is my Firstest Friend!

readings.title: The Butterfly That Stamped, part 1: A wise king who stopped showing off
readings.challenge: Find one proof for each of three things the narrator says about the king.
readings.focus: Before the real story begins, a great king learns that showing off is silly.
readings.context: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, India, and made up the Just So Stories (1902) as bedtime stories for his own children; “Best Beloved” is the child listening. Each story explains, in a made-up and joking way, how something came to be as it is. They are called “Just So” because his daughter wanted them told exactly the same way every time, so read every word. This story is not about how an animal got its shape. Suleiman-bin-Daoud is the Arabic name of King Solomon, son of King David, a wise king in the Bible and the Quran; many old stories, especially Arabic and Persian ones, tell of his magic ring and his power over Djinns (genies) and Afrits (powerful spirits). Balkis is their name for the Queen of Sheba. A sovereign is a king or queen. “From the bishop on the bench to the hyssop on the wall” means everything, great and small; hyssop is a little herb. Azrael is a great angel in old Jewish and Islamic legends. “O King, live for ever” is an old polite way to speak to a king.
readings.contentNote: Kipling borrows King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba from the Bible, the Quran and old legends and plays with them; this is a made-up story, not a religious teaching.

excerpt.locator: “The Butterfly That Stamped,” from the beginning to the story of the Animal that ate the dinner, ending “now the real story part of my story begins”; opens “THIS, O my Best Beloved, is a story—a new and a wonderful story—a story quite different…”; closes “…forgot that it was silly to show off; and now the real story part of my story begins.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator begins by naming stories he will not tell. Why might a storyteller do that?
facilitatorNotes: He lists the Lapwing, the Hoopoe, the Glass Pavement and more before saying this is the story of the Butterfly that Stamped. It teases the listener with other mysteries and makes this one feel special. Some children will want to hear the others too!
evidence: There are three hundred and fifty-five stories about Suleiman-bin-Daoud; but this is not one of them.

questions.prompt: Kipling says three things about Suleiman-bin-Daoud: he was wise, he was strong, and he was not proud. Find one proof of each.
facilitatorNotes: Wise: he understood beasts, birds, fishes, insects, rocks and trees. Strong: turning his ring called up Djinns, Fairies and a great angel. Not proud: he seldom showed off, and was sorry when he did.
evidence: He understood what the beasts said, what the birds said, what the fishes said, and what the insects said.
When he turned it once, Afrits and Djinns came out of the earth to do whatever he told them.
He very seldom showed off, and when he did he was sorry for it.

questions.prompt: What went wrong with the king’s dinner for all the animals in the world? Why is the Animal’s answer funny?
facilitatorNotes: One Animal from the sea ate it all in three mouthfuls, then said it was the smallest of thirty thousand brothers, who each eat twice as much between meals. The king’s enormous feast was hardly a snack.
evidence: I am the smallest of thirty thousand brothers,
do you really call that a dinner?

questions.prompt: What lesson does Suleiman-bin-Daoud take from the Animal? Does it matter why we do a good deed, or only that we do it?
facilitatorNotes: He admits he gave the dinner to show how great and rich he was, not out of real kindness, and resolves never to show off again. Readers can argue both sides: the animals would still have been fed, but the king himself thinks his reason made it wrong.
evidence: I gave that dinner to show what a great and rich king I was, and not because I really wanted to be kind to the animals.
After that he never forgot that it was silly to show off;

readings.title: The Butterfly That Stamped, part 2: A thousand quarrels and one boast
readings.challenge: Compare what really happened with the way a boaster retells it.
readings.focus: A king who will not use his power for himself meets a tiny creature who pretends to have power he lacks.
readings.context: Recap: King Suleiman-bin-Daoud (Solomon) is wise and has a ring that calls up Djinns, but ever since a sea-Animal ate a dinner he gave only to show off, he has refused to show off again. Balkis is his Head Queen. Camphor-trees, loquats and cannas grow in warm countries. Presumption is boldness that goes too far; a fib is a small lie; impudence is cheek.
readings.contentNote: Kipling borrows King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba from the Bible, the Quran and old legends and plays with them; this is a made-up story, not a religious teaching. In the old stories kings like Solomon had a great many wives, and the story says it was the custom “in those days.” Its jokes about husbands and wives belong to Kipling’s time.

excerpt.locator: “The Butterfly That Stamped,” from the nine hundred and ninety-nine wives to Suleiman-bin-Daoud laughing at the Butterfly’s impudence; opens “He married ever so many wifes. He married nine hundred and ninety-nine wives, besides the…”; closes “…laughed till the tears ran down his face at the impudence of the bad little Butterfly.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Suleiman-bin-Daoud marry nine hundred and ninety-nine wives, and what was the trouble with them?
facilitatorNotes: Everybody married many wives then, and the King married more “just to show that he was the King.” Some were horrid, made the nice ones horrid too, and all quarrelled with him. Notice the irony: he married them to show off, the very thing he tries not to do.
evidence: just to show that he was the King.
the horrid ones quarrelled with the nice ones and made them horrid too,

questions.prompt: Why won’t he use his ring to stop the quarrelling, even when Balkis asks him to?
facilitatorNotes: It would be showing off, and he remembers the Animal that made him ashamed; he says he will “endure my fate.” Is that wise, or only stubborn? Both answers can be argued.
evidence: remember the Animal that came out of the sea and made me ashamed
I shall continue to endure my fate

questions.prompt: What does the Butterfly boast to his wife? Why does the King laugh “till the camphor-tree shook”?
facilitatorNotes: That one stamp of his foot would make the Palace and the garden vanish in a clap of thunder. A butterfly’s stamp would not bend a blade of grass, so the boast is absurd, and the King forgets his troubles laughing.
evidence: if I stamped with my foot all Suleiman-bin-Daoud's Palace and this garden here would immediately vanish in a clap of thunder.
you know that all your stamping wouldn't bend one blade of grass.

questions.prompt: Back with his wife, how does the Butterfly retell what happened? What has he changed?
facilitatorNotes: He says he meant the King to hear him, and that the King asked him not to stamp, as if the King were afraid of him. In fact the King laughed at him. He is saving face; children can retell what really happened.
evidence: Of course he did. I meant him to hear me.
he asked me not to stamp, and I promised I wouldn't.

questions.prompt: Balkis hides among the irises behind the tree. What does that tell you about her? What do you predict she will do?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to be near the King, is truly sorry for him, and is nearly as wise as he is. Readers may predict that she will find a way to deal with the quarrelling Queens.
evidence: so as to be near her own true love, Suleiman-bin-Daoud.
was truly sorry for him.

readings.title: The Butterfly That Stamped, part 3: Stamp! Stamp! Stamp!
readings.challenge: Follow a plan made by one character and carried out, without his knowing it, by another.
readings.focus: Balkis turns the Butterfly’s boast into a lesson, and the King uses his ring for a joke.
readings.context: Recap: King Suleiman-bin-Daoud has a magic ring but will not show off, so his nine hundred and ninety-nine quarrelling wives give him no peace. In his garden he heard a Butterfly boast that one stamp of his foot could make the Palace vanish; the King laughed, and the Butterfly told his wife the King had begged him not to stamp. Queen Balkis heard it all from her hiding-place. To humour someone is to go along with him to keep him happy; mirth is laughter.
readings.contentNote: Kipling borrows King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba from the Bible, the Quran and old legends and plays with them; this is a made-up story, not a religious teaching. The King calls the Djinns “Slaves”; in these old tales the spirits of the ring must serve whoever holds it.

excerpt.locator: “The Butterfly That Stamped,” from Balkis calling the Butterfly’s Wife to the Palace coming back down; opens “Balkis the Most Beautiful stood up behind the tree among the red lilies and smiled to…”; closes “…is the sense of returning to me my Palace if at the same time you slay me with mirth!'”.

questions.prompt: What advice does Balkis give the Butterfly’s Wife, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Next time he boasts, take him at his word and ask him to stamp. Balkis hopes it will make the King use his magic and so save him from the quarrelsome Queens.
evidence: next time he begins to boast, take him at his word. Ask him to stamp,
If I am wise I can yet save my Lord from the persecutions of these quarrelsome Queens,

questions.prompt: Why does Suleiman-bin-Daoud finally turn his ring? Is that showing off?
facilitatorNotes: For the little Butterfly’s sake, so his wife will not laugh at him for ever, and “not for the sake of showing off.” Some readers call it kindness; others say the King mostly enjoys the joke. Both fit the text.
evidence: just for the little Butterfly's sake, not for the sake of showing off,

questions.prompt: Describe what happens at the first stamp, and at the second.
facilitatorNotes: The Djinns jerk the Palace and gardens a thousand miles into the air, with thunder and inky darkness, and the wife cries that she will be good. At the second stamp they set everything down “without even a bump,” and the birds go on singing.
evidence: The Djinns jerked the Palace and the gardens a thousand miles into the air:
without even a bump.

questions.prompt: How does the Butterfly talk after the first stamp? What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He blames his wife’s nagging and pretends he is used to such magic, though he is nearly as frightened as she is. He is still boasting, which makes the King laugh even more.
evidence: Of course it doesn't make any difference to me—I'm used to this kind of thing—
The Butterfly was nearly as frightened as his wife,

questions.prompt: The King calls the Butterfly “most great magician” and “great wizard.” Does he mean it? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: No: he can hardly breathe for laughing and says the Butterfly may “slay me with mirth.” Playing along with the boast is part of the joke.
evidence: Give me back my Palace, most great magician.
what is the sense of returning to me my Palace if at the same time you slay me with mirth!

readings.title: The Butterfly That Stamped, part 4: Balkis the Wise
readings.challenge: Decide who really solved the King’s problem, and what the closing poem admires.
readings.focus: The quarrelling Queens are frightened into quiet, and the King learns whose wisdom freed him.
readings.context: Recap: King Suleiman-bin-Daoud will not use his magic ring to show off, so his nine hundred and ninety-nine wives quarrel without end. Queen Balkis, hidden in the garden, told a Butterfly’s wife to dare her boastful husband to stamp his foot; for a joke, the King had his Djinns lift the whole Palace into the air at the first stamp and set it down at the second. Now the frightened Queens come running out. Abreast means side by side; statelily means in a grand, dignified way; noisome means nasty. Sheba, or Sabæa, was an old kingdom in southern Arabia; felicity means happiness.
readings.contentNote: Kipling borrows King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba from the Bible, the Quran and old legends and plays with them; this is a made-up story, not a religious teaching. The Queens are frightened into being “mousy-quiet,” and the story praises “low-speaking and humbleness” in wives; those ideas about how women should behave belong to Kipling’s time. The wisest person in the story is a woman.

excerpt.locator: “The Butterfly That Stamped,” from the Queens running out of the Palace to the end, with the closing verses; opens “Then came a terrible noise, for all the nine hundred and ninety-nine Queens ran out of…”; closes “…Lord— But they both of 'em talked to butterflies When they took their walks abroad!”.

questions.prompt: How do the Queens describe their trouble? Read their speech aloud. Which word do they keep using?
facilitatorNotes: Trouble: “troubled,” “troublesome,” “trouble” again and again. The Palace vanished, they sat in darkness, it thundered and Djinns moved about. Kipling makes the speech funny with the repeats.
evidence: it was a troublesome trouble, unlike any trouble we have known.

questions.prompt: How does Balkis explain what happened? How do the King’s words to the Butterflies seem to prove it to the Queens?
facilitatorNotes: She says the King was teaching the Butterfly’s wife a lesson for quarrelling. Then the Queens hear him tell the wife to please her husband “lest he be provoked to stamp his foot yet again.” He is joking, but the Queens take it seriously and fear what he would do to them.
evidence: it has pleased our Lord Suleiman-bin-Daoud to teach her a lesson
If these things are done when a Butterfly is displeased with his wife, what shall be done to us

questions.prompt: The Egyptian Queen doubts Balkis. What does she think happened, and how does Balkis answer?
facilitatorNotes: She says a palace cannot be plucked up like a leek for an insect, so the King must be dead. Balkis does not argue; she says “Come and see.” Showing is stronger than arguing.
evidence: Our Palace cannot be plucked up by the roots like a leek for the sake of a little insect.
Come and see.

questions.prompt: Who really solved the King’s problem? Did he know he was solving it?
facilitatorNotes: Balkis planned it; the King was only joking with a Butterfly and learned the rest when she told him. He says her wisdom let him use magic for a jest instead of for pride. So the narrator asks, “But wasn’t it clever of Balkis?”
evidence: For I have been jesting with a Butterfly ever since I came into the garden.
But wasn't it clever of Balkis?

questions.prompt: What two reasons does Balkis give for being wise? What does the closing poem say the great Queen and King both did, and why might it admire that?
facilitatorNotes: Because she loved him, and because she knows what women-folk are. The poem says the greatest Queen and King both talked to butterflies as to friends: being great and being kind to small creatures go together. Readers may find other things the poem admires.
evidence: First, O my Lord, because I loved you;
But they both of 'em talked to butterflies
